summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2 / Grades 2-4): social insects — how ants and bees live and work together in colonies. The central idea is DIVISION OF LABOUR: different members (queen, workers, drones) do different jobs (forage, build, guard, nurse), and the whole colony survives because jobs are shared in a way no single insect could manage. Key corrections: the queen lays eggs but does not command the colony (it self-organises on instinctive roles); not every insect does the same job; drones are males whose main role is mating; a lone social insect cannot thrive as the colony does. The strongest proposed learning puts the child in charge of allocating members to jobs and watching the colony thrive or struggle; supporting activities label nest/hive structure, assess role-interdependence, let children explore roles in-role, and transfer the idea from an ant nest to a bee hive. Parallels to human teamwork are useful but the hierarchy analogy should be flagged as imperfect. These are research-informed proposals, not validated or verified against re-fetched sources.
misconceptions: 'The queen rules and gives orders' — she is the egg-layer; the colony self-organises without a boss.
'Every insect in the colony does the same thing' — the point is different members do different jobs.
'Drones do the work' — drones are males whose main role is mating; workers do the labour.
'One ant/bee could survive fine alone' — social insects depend on the colony.
'Bees and ants are led like a human team with a manager' — the analogy overstates hierarchy.

activities.title: Run the colony: share out the jobs
steps: Take charge of a colony shown as a cutaway nest or hive with live meters for food, defence, and new baby insects (brood).
Decide how to deploy the workers across roles — foragers, builders, guards, nurses — for example by dragging members onto jobs or adjusting how many do each task.
Send lots of workers out to forage and watch the food meter climb; notice that with no one on guard a raider slips in and the brood suffers.
Rebalance: assign a few guards, some nurses, and some foragers, and watch the colony settle into a healthy state.
Use a 'pull one role out' probe: remove every nurse and see that the young are not fed, so no new workers grow up; remove the foragers and see the food run out until the colony starves.
Tap the queen (in her chamber in the ant nest, or on the brood comb in the hive) to check her real job — she lays eggs, she does not bark orders.
activities.insight: A colony survives because its members divide up the jobs: no single ant or bee could do everything, but the team together can. Each role matters, so removing one job makes the whole colony struggle.

activities.title: Cutaway nest and hive: who does what, and where
steps: Explore a cross-section (cutaway) of an ant nest (tunnels and chambers such as a nursery, food stores and often a chamber where the queen stays) or a bee hive (wax comb with brood cells for eggs and young, and cells storing honey and pollen; the queen moves across the brood comb rather than living in one chamber).
Tap or point to each chamber and role to reveal its job and how it fits into the whole colony.
Match each member — queen, worker, drone — to what it does, and note that drones are males whose main role is mating while workers do the labour.
Say in your own words how the organised structure of the nest reflects the different jobs being done.
activities.insight: A colony is an organised home with distinct chambers and roles — the structure you can see reflects the different jobs that keep the colony running.

activities.title: A day in the hive: ask a worker about its jobs
steps: Interview a worker bee (in role) about the different jobs it does through its life — cleaning, nursing the young, building comb, guarding, and foraging.
Ask what would happen to the hive if no bees did one of those jobs.
Ask whether the queen tells the worker what to do, and compare the answer to what you expected.
activities.insight: Each worker takes on several jobs that the colony needs, and does so without being commanded — building a fuller picture of how the colony self-organises.

activities.title: Check your thinking: roles and what fails without them
steps: Answer the diagnostic: 'In an ant nest there is a queen and lots of worker ants. Someone says: The queen is the boss — she tells all the other ants what to do. Is that right? Tell me what the queen actually does and what the workers do, and why living together in a colony helps the ants.'
Match each member to its role (queen to laying eggs; worker to foraging/building/guarding/nursing).
Answer a consequence question: 'What happens to the colony if there are no foragers at all?'
Answer the follow-up: 'Why does living together in a colony help, compared with one ant on its own?'
Name two DIFFERENT jobs in the colony and say why it helps that they are different.
Transfer the idea: 'A bee hive also has a queen and workers. Is a hive organised like the ant nest, or differently?'
activities.insight: Children who understand social insects give the queen the egg-laying role (not a command role), explain that dividing up the jobs lets the colony do more than any single ant could, and recognise that a bee hive is organised in the same division-of-labour way.

checkQuestion: In an ant nest there is a queen, and lots of worker ants. Someone says: 'The queen is the boss — she tells all the other ants what to do.' Is that right? Tell me what the queen actually does and what the workers do, and why living together in a colony helps the ants.
checkAnswer: It's not really right — the queen is not a boss giving orders. Her main job is to lay the eggs. The worker ants do the other jobs: finding food, building and cleaning tunnels, caring for eggs and young, and guarding the nest. Living together in a colony helps because the jobs are shared out (division of labour) — no single ant has to do everything, so the whole colony survives better than one ant could alone.
